content: The palatine tonsils are visible structures located at the back of the throat. They are part of the immune system and play a significant role in local immunity. Tonsillitis refers to the inflammation of the tonsils, which often causes symptoms such as a sore throat and fever. In chronic or severe cases, surgical removal of the tonsils, known as a tonsillectomy, may be necessary. Functions of Palatine Tonsils Local Immunity The B cells within the palatine tonsils are capable of maturing to produce all five major classes of immunoglobulins (Ig). When stimulated in vitro with mitogens or specific antigens, these B cells generate antibodies against pathogens such as diphtheria toxoid, poliovirus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and lipopolysaccharides of Escherichia coli. Most of the IgA produced by tonsillar B cells in vitro is in the form of 7S monomers, although a smaller proportion exists as 10S dimeric IgA. In addition to humoral immunity, the tonsils elicit a robust T-cell response upon antigenic stimulation. For example, natural infection or intranasal immunization with live attenuated rubella virus has been shown to prime tonsillar lymphocytes more effectively than subcutaneous vaccination. Similarly, natural infection with varicella-zoster virus stimulates tonsillar lymphocytes more effectively than peripheral blood lymphocytes. However, combined tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy significantly impair the local IgA response in the nasopharyngeal fluid, particularly against poliovirus. This immunological deficit correlates with an increased incidence of paralytic poliomyelitis following the procedure. These findings underscore the critical role of the palatine tonsils in defending against bacterial and viral infections. The success of mucosal immunity induced by intranasal vaccines likely depends on the immunocompetent tissues of the oropharynx and nasopharynx. However, in cases of recurrent tonsillitis, persistent antigenic stimulation may overwhelm the tonsillar lymphocytes, impairing their ability to respond to new antigens. This immunological dysfunction compromises the tonsils' protective role and their ability to support the secretory immune system of the upper respiratory tract. Cytokine Action Cytokines are immunomodulatory proteins or glycoproteins that regulate the activity of target cells, leading to processes such as gene activation, mitosis, growth, differentiation, migration, or apoptosis. They are produced by various cell types in response to both antigen-specific and non-specific stimuli. The balance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines influences the clinical outcomes of many infectious, autoimmune, and malignant diseases. Studies of cytokine profiles in the tonsils provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying these conditions. The palatine tonsils are active immunological organs containing a diverse array of cytokine-producing cells. Both Th1 and Th2 cytokines, as well as their mRNA, are detectable in conditions such as tonsillar hypertrophy (TH) and recurrent tonsillitis (RT). This suggests that both Th1 and Th2 cells contribute to the pathophysiology of these conditions. Even in asymptomatic individuals, the tonsils harbor microbial antigens, which may reflect the ontogeny of the immune system. Anatomy of the Palatine Tonsils The palatine tonsils are part of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) and are located at the entrance to the upper respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. Their strategic position allows them to protect the body from exogenous material entering through mucosal sites. However, this location also makes them susceptible to infections and inflammation. The palatine tonsils are a key component of Waldeyer's ring, which includes the nasopharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), paired tubal tonsils, paired palatine tonsils, and the lingual tonsil. In children, the palatine tonsils are common sites of infection, leading to acute or chronic tonsillitis. The role of persistent infection in causing tonsillar hypertrophy remains unclear. Tonsillectomy is a frequently performed surgical procedure in children, but its indications are debated due to the potential harm of removing an important immune-inductive tissue. Tonsillar Crypts The palatine tonsils contain an extensive system of crypts, which significantly increase their internal surface area. These crypts are lined by stratified squamous epithelium and extend deep into the tonsil, creating a complex network. The crypt system enhances the interaction between environmental antigens and the lymphoid tissue, facilitating early immune responses. The epithelial surface area of the crypts in an average adult tonsil is approximately 295 cm², in addition to the 45 cm² of epithelium covering the oropharyngeal surface. The crypts are surrounded by blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and germinal centers, and they are rich in macrophages and other immune cells. This arrangement allows the crypts to serve as a forward sentry for the immune system, exposing immune cells to potential pathogens introduced through food or other ingested material. However, the crypts can also become sites of bacterial overgrowth, leading to the formation of tonsilloliths (tonsil stones). These small, whitish plugs can cause bad breath, throat irritation, and a sensation of something being stuck in the throat. Diseases of the Palatine Tonsils Acute Tonsillitis Acute tonsillitis is the most common tonsillar disease and is characterized by inflammation of the tonsils. Symptoms include sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). The tonsils may appear erythematous and may or may not have exudates. Not all symptoms are present in every case. Recurrent Tonsillitis Recurrent tonsillitis is defined as multiple episodes of acute tonsillitis over a specific period. Criteria include four to seven episodes in one year, five episodes per year for two consecutive years, or three episodes per year for three consecutive years. Tonsillar Hypertrophy Tonsillar hypertrophy refers to the enlargement of the tonsils without a history of inflammation. Obstructive tonsillar hypertrophy is the most common indication for tonsillectomy. Symptoms include loud snoring, irregular breathing during sleep, nocturnal choking or coughing, restless sleep, daytime hypersomnolence, dysphagia, and behavioral changes. Conclusion The palatine tonsils are critical components of the immune system, particularly in the oropharynx. They play a vital role in local immunity and cytokine production, but their anatomical location and function also make them susceptible to infections and inflammation. Understanding the immunological and anatomical features of the tonsils is essential for managing tonsillar diseases and determining the indications for tonsillectomy.
